## Virtual Machine Operator Agent

**Status:** production
**Category:** Tool Use & Environment
**Authors:** Nikola Balic (@nibzard)
**Source:** https://www.nibzard.com/silent-revolution

## Problem

AI agents need to perform complex tasks beyond simple code generation or text manipulation. They require the ability to interact with a full computer environment to execute code, manage system resources, install software, and operate various applications.

## Solution

Equip the AI agent with access to a dedicated virtual machine (VM) environment. The agent is trained or designed to understand how to operate within this VM, treating it as its direct workspace. This allows the agent to:

- Execute arbitrary code and scripts.
- Install and manage software packages.
- Read from and write to the file system.
- Utilize other command-line tools and applications available within the VM.

This pattern transforms the agent from a specialized tool into a more general-purpose digital operator.

Common implementation approaches include:

- **Full virtual machines** (EC2, GCP) - Maximum isolation, higher overhead
- **MicroVMs** (Firecracker, Modal, E2B) - Balanced isolation with fast startup
- **Container isolation** (Docker, Kubernetes) - Faster startup, shared kernel risk
- **Tool-mediated execution** - Minimal overhead, capability-scoped

## Example (flow)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Agent
    participant VM as Virtual Machine

    User->>Agent: Complex Task Request
    Agent->>VM: Execute Code/Scripts
    Agent->>VM: Install Packages
    Agent->>VM: File System Operations
    Agent->>VM: Use CLI Tools/Apps
    VM-->>Agent: Execution Results
    Agent->>Agent: Process & Analyze Results
    Agent-->>User: Task Completion Report
```

## How to use it

- Pick the isolation level to match the workload: full VMs for untrusted or long-lived work, microVMs or containers for fast per-task sandboxes.
- Give the agent a scoped entry point (shell, file API, or screen) rather than raw host access, and snapshot or reset the filesystem between sessions.
- Budget for cold starts: keep warm pools or reuse a session for multi-step tasks instead of provisioning per call.
- Log everything that runs inside the machine so results and failures can be audited after the fact.
- Enforce hard execution limits (CPU, wall-clock, network egress) outside the VM, not by trusting the agent to stop.

## Trade-offs

* **Pros:** Gives the agent a full general-purpose environment (code execution, package installs, CLI tools) with strong isolation from the host; failures stay inside the disposable machine.
* **Cons:** Cold-start latency and per-hour compute cost; environment upkeep (images, dependencies); screen- or shell-mediated operation is slower and more error-prone than purpose-built tools.

## References

- Amjad Masad (Replit), speaking at a Village Global event: "People think of computer use as something like an operator, but actually it is more like you give the model a virtual machine, and it knows how to execute code on it, install packages, write scripts, use apps, do as much as possible with the computer." Quoted as recounted in [How AI Agents Are Reshaping Creation](https://www.nibzard.com/silent-revolution), a secondary summary that states over 90% of its text was AI-generated; Amjad Masad: https://x.com/amasad

- Anthropic computer use tool documentation - production API for agents that operate a computer (screenshots, cursor, keyboard): https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool

- E2B - sandbox microVM provider for running agent-generated code: https://e2b.dev

- Modal - sandboxed cloud containers for agent code execution: https://modal.com

- Beurer-Kellner et al. (2025). "Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents." arXiv:2506.08837 - Comprehensive framework for secure LLM agent execution including Action Selector and Code-Then-Execute patterns.

- Yao et al. (2022). "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models." arXiv:2210.03629 - Foundational reasoning-acting paradigm (Thought → Action → Observation).

## Visual AI Multimodal Integration

**Status:** production
**Category:** Tool Use & Environment
**Authors:** Nikola Balic (@nibzard)
**Source:** https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool

## Problem

Many real-world tasks require understanding and processing visual information alongside text. Traditional text-only agents miss critical information present in images, videos, diagrams, and visual interfaces. This limitation prevents agents from helping with tasks like analyzing screenshots, debugging UI issues, understanding charts, processing security footage, or working with visual documentation.

## Solution

Integrate large multimodal models (LMMs) into agent architectures to enable visual understanding capabilities. Vision input is now a default capability of frontier models, so the pattern is the integration architecture around it — input pipelines, the screenshot-driven agent loop, and cost control — not the presence of vision itself. This pattern involves:

1. **Visual Input Handling**: Accept images, videos, or screenshots as input alongside text. Images are typically resized and base64-encoded or provided via URL. Video often requires frame extraction unless the chosen provider accepts video natively.

2. **Visual Analysis**: Use multimodal models to extract information, identify objects, read text (OCR), understand spatial relationships, and interpret diagrams or charts.

3. **Cross-Modal Reasoning**: Combine visual and textual information for comprehensive understanding, enabling tasks like UI debugging from screenshots or data extraction from charts.

4. **Visual-Guided Actions**: Take actions based on visual understanding (clicking UI elements, describing scenes, counting objects).

**Provider Selection**: Current frontier models from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI all accept image input, so select by task fit and current benchmarks rather than by vision support alone. For screenshot-driven computer use, Anthropic ships a documented computer-use tool (see References); open-source multimodal models such as LLaVA remain an option for self-hosted deployments.

## Example

```python
class VisualAIAgent:
    def __init__(self, multimodal_llm, text_llm=None):
        self.mm_llm = multimodal_llm
        self.text_llm = text_llm or multimodal_llm
        
    async def process_visual_task(self, task_description, visual_inputs):
        # Analyze each visual input
        visual_analyses = []
        for visual in visual_inputs:
            analysis = await self.analyze_visual(visual, task_description)
            visual_analyses.append(analysis)
        
        # Combine visual analyses with task
        combined_context = self.merge_visual_context(
            task_description, 
            visual_analyses
        )
        
        # Generate solution using combined understanding
        return await self.solve_with_visual_context(combined_context)
    
    async def analyze_visual(self, visual_input, context):
        prompt = f"""
        Task context: {context}
        
        Analyze this {visual_input.type} and extract:
        1. Relevant objects and their positions
        2. Any text present (OCR)
        3. Colors, patterns, or visual indicators
        4. Spatial relationships
        5. Anything relevant to the task
        
        Provide structured analysis:
        """
        
        return await self.mm_llm.analyze(
            prompt=prompt,
            image=visual_input.data
        )
    
    async def solve_with_visual_context(self, context):
        return await self.text_llm.generate(f"""
        Based on the visual analysis and task requirements:
        {context}
        
        Provide a comprehensive solution that incorporates 
        the visual information.
        """)

# Specialized visual agents for specific domains
class UIDebugAgent(VisualAIAgent):
    async def debug_ui_issue(self, screenshot, issue_description):
        ui_analysis = await self.analyze_visual(
            screenshot, 
            f"UI debugging: {issue_description}"
        )
        
        return await self.mm_llm.generate(f"""
        UI Analysis: {ui_analysis}
        Issue: {issue_description}
        
        Identify:
        1. Potential UI problems visible in the screenshot
        2. Specific elements that might cause the issue
        3. Recommendations for fixes
        4. Exact coordinates or selectors if applicable
        """)

class VideoAnalysisAgent(VisualAIAgent):
    async def analyze_video_segment(self, video_path, query):
        # Process video in chunks
        key_frames = await self.extract_key_frames(video_path)
        
        frame_analyses = []
        for frame in key_frames:
            analysis = await self.analyze_visual(frame, query)
            frame_analyses.append({
                'timestamp': frame.timestamp,
                'analysis': analysis
            })
        
        # Temporal reasoning across frames
        return await self.temporal_reasoning(frame_analyses, query)
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User Query + Visual Input] --> B{Input Type}
    
    B -->|Image| C[Image Analysis]
    B -->|Video| D[Video Processing]
    B -->|Screenshot| E[UI Analysis]
    
    C --> F[Object Detection]
    C --> G[OCR/Text Extraction]
    C --> H[Spatial Understanding]
    
    D --> I[Key Frame Extraction]
    I --> J[Frame-by-Frame Analysis]
    J --> K[Temporal Reasoning]
    
    E --> L[Element Identification]
    E --> M[Layout Analysis]
    
    F --> N[Multimodal Integration]
    G --> N
    H --> N
    K --> N
    L --> N
    M --> N
    
    N --> O[Combined Understanding]
    O --> P[Task Solution]
    
    style B fill:#e1f5fe,stroke:#01579b,stroke-width:2px
    style N fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#4a148c,stroke-width:2px
```

## Use Cases

- **UI/UX Debugging**: Analyze screenshots to identify visual bugs or usability issues
- **Document Processing**: Extract information from charts, diagrams, and visual documents
- **Video Analysis**: Count objects, identify events, or generate timestamps in videos
- **Security Monitoring**: Analyze security footage for specific activities or anomalies
- **Medical Imaging**: Assist in analyzing medical images (with appropriate disclaimers)
- **E-commerce**: Analyze product images for categorization or quality control

## How to use it

- Use when tasks require visual understanding—UI debugging, document processing, image analysis, video comprehension, or code generation from screenshots.

- **Choose provider by use case**: all frontier providers accept images, so pick by task fit and verify current capability against the provider's own documentation (for example Anthropic's computer-use tool for screenshot-driven agents, or an open-source multimodal model for self-hosting).

- **Optimize for costs**: Resize images to minimum viable size, use appropriate detail levels (low for general understanding, high for OCR), and consider cascading approaches (smaller models first, escalate when needed).

## Trade-offs

**Pros:**

- Enables entirely new categories of tasks
- More natural interaction (users can show rather than describe)
- Better accuracy for visual tasks
- Can handle complex multimodal reasoning

**Cons:**

- Higher computational costs for visual processing
- Larger model requirements
- Potential privacy concerns with visual data
- May require specialized infrastructure for video processing
- Quality depends on visual model capabilities

## References

- Primary source: [Claude computer-use tool documentation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool) — describes a shipped, screenshot-driven multimodal agent loop: the agent returns tool-use blocks such as screenshot, click, and type; the host executes them in a sandbox and returns tool results, repeating until the task completes.
- [GPT-4V(ision) System Card](https://openai.com/research/gpt-4v-system-card) — OpenAI's 2023 safety analysis of an early vision model; useful background on visual-capability risks, not a description of this pattern.
- [LLaVA: Visual Instruction Tuning (Liu et al., 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485) — early open-source multimodal instruction-following model; historical baseline for self-hosted visual agents.
- Earlier revisions linked a generic newsletter index and provider marketing pages in place of pattern sources; they were removed or replaced with the pages above.

## Voice Agent Turn-Taking & Barge-In Handling

**Status:** production
**Category:** UX & Collaboration
**Authors:** Nikola Balic (@nibzard)
**Source:** https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat

## Problem

A chat loop gets turn-taking for free. The user submits a message, and the agent replies after that. Live audio has no submit event. From a sound stream, the agent must decide when the user has finished and when the user has cut in.

[Chain-of-Thought Monitoring & Interruption](chain-of-thought-monitoring-interruption.md) gives the user a stop button for reasoning that the user can read. A voice channel has no button. The user speaks, and the agent must recognize that speech as a stop signal.

The common port of a chat loop to audio uses one voice activity detector (VAD) and a silence timer. It fails in three ways:

- **It cuts users off.** A pause after "I'd like to book..." starts the reply, and the agent talks over the rest of the sentence.
- **It stops for anything.** A cough, a door, or a listener's "uh-huh" counts as speech, so the agent stops in the middle of an answer.
- **It answers words that nobody heard.** After the agent is cut off, its complete reply stays in the conversation history. The next reply assumes that the user heard all of it.

A fourth defect appears when the agent calls a tool. Speech stops, the caller hears silence, and many callers start to speak again or hang up.

## Solution

Run four control loops in one pipeline. Each loop corrects one defect. The loops share three signals: the audio playout clock, the transcript, and the cancellation state.

1. **Two-stage endpointing.** A fast acoustic VAD finds speech and silence. A semantic end-of-turn detector then reads the partial transcript and the acoustic properties of the speech. It decides whether the thought is complete or the speaker paused in the middle of a clause. The turn ends when the detector reports a complete turn and the final transcript is available. A maximum delay closes the turn when the detector does not decide.
2. **Adaptive barge-in and pipeline flush.** Speech that arrives during playback goes through a second decision: noise or backchannel, or a real interruption. A real interruption emits a high-priority cancel signal. The signal stops TTS synthesis, clears the output audio buffers, and aborts LLM generation and each speculative reply.
3. **Playback-offset transcript reconciliation.** The pipeline tracks how much of the reply reached the user's speaker when the interruption arrived. It uses the timestamps of the TTS segments to map that duration to a text offset. Then it cuts the assistant message in the conversation history down to that spoken prefix.
4. **Tool-call latency masking.** When a tool call is slower than a threshold, the agent says one short line, such as "Let me check that for you", and runs the tool asynchronously. The line reports no result and makes no promise.

The start and the end of a turn need opposite treatment. A barge-in must be fast, so its cancel signal outranks the frames that wait in the queue. The end of a turn must be correct, so it waits for the final transcript.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["User audio"] --> V["VAD: speech and silence"]
    U --> S["STT: partial and final transcript"]
    V --> E["Semantic end-of-turn detector"]
    S --> E
    E -->|"complete turn and final transcript"| R["LLM and tool calls"]
    R --> T["TTS playback"]
    V -->|"speech during playback"| B{"Noise, backchannel, or real interruption?"}
    B -->|"noise or backchannel"| T
    B -->|"real interruption"| X["Cancel: flush audio, stop TTS, abort LLM"]
    X --> P["Cut the assistant message to the played prefix"]
    P --> U
    R -->|"tool slower than the threshold"| H["Short filler: no result, no promise"]
    H --> T
```

```pseudo
on_user_speech_started():                    # from VAD: speech, noise, or echo
    if not agent.is_speaking(): return       # a normal turn start
    if not real_interruption(audio, interim_transcript):
        return                               # noise, backchannel, or echo
    agent.interrupt()                        # outranks queued frames, aborts the LLM
    played_ms = player.playout_position()    # audio that reached the speaker
    history.replace(agent.reply, spoken_prefix(agent.reply, played_ms))

async on_silence(interim_transcript, elapsed):
    complete = turn_detector.complete(interim_transcript)
    if not complete and elapsed < max_delay: return   # the speaker may continue
    reply = await run_llm_and_tools(final_transcript())
    agent.say(reply)

async run_llm_and_tools(text):
    call = start_tool_call(text)             # receives the cancellation signal
    done = await race(call, timer(filler_delay))
    if done is timer:                        # the tool is slow: mask the silence
        say_cached("Let me check that for you.")      # no facts, no promises
    return await call
```

## Evidence

- **Evidence Grade:** `high` (two independent open-source frameworks ship these mechanisms and document the failure modes)
- **Most Valuable Findings:**
  - The turn detector of LiveKit "Predicts end of turn from both the meaning of speech and its acoustic properties, on top of VAD". Its VAD-only mode is for "minimal latency" or for a language that the model does not cover.
  - LiveKit describes the history fix directly: "When interrupted, the agent stops speaking and automatically truncates its conversation history to include only the portion of the speech that the user heard before interruption". In its source, each TTS audio frame carries timed text, and an interrupted segment reports its playback position. The text that stays is "The text that actually reached the user, accounting for interruptions".
  - The adaptive interruption mode of LiveKit "uses an audio model to distinguish real interruptions from backchannel acknowledgments". Its tuning guide lists "Agent cuts users off mid-thought" and "Agent is interrupted by short acknowledgments" as common symptoms.
  - Pipecat processes an `InterruptionFrame` as a system frame. System frames outrank data and control frames in the queue of each processor, and the interruption cancels the current tasks of that processor.
  - A tool is not stopped by the interruption in LiveKit: "A tool continues running in the background until it returns". For work that "takes more than a few seconds", its guide recommends an async tool, so that "the agent can keep talking and send progress updates while the tool runs".
  - For the wait, LiveKit shows "a pre-synthesized hold message" that "avoids TTS latency during tool execution". Pipecat ships the remark for a long wait as an optional extension, `WaitReassuranceLLMExtension`. Its default interval is 10 seconds of quiet, and it instructs the model: "Never report a result or a finding, never say the work is done, and ask no questions and make no offers or promises".
- **Unverified / Unclear:** No source measures the effect of the hold message or gives a threshold for it. The interval of 10 seconds of Pipecat is the quiet time before a progress remark, not before the first acknowledgement. No source gives accuracy figures for the turn and interruption models. LiveKit licenses its turn detection models under a separate model license, and self-hosted use of adaptive mode counts toward a monthly development allowance.

## How to use it

1. **Start from the framework defaults.** LiveKit enables the turn detector by default, with an endpointing minimum delay of 0.5 seconds and a maximum of 3.0 seconds. Tune from measurements, not by feel.
2. **Keep two detectors.** Use VAD for barge-in, because it is fast. Use the semantic detector for end of turn, because it must be correct. Do not use one model for both jobs.
3. **Gate the barge-in.** Require a minimum speech duration or a minimum number of transcribed words before an interruption counts. Resume the reply from the cut point when an interruption was false.
4. **Flush on each interruption.** Stop TTS, clear the audio buffers, and abort LLM generation, speculative replies, and the speech that waits in the queue.
5. **Reconcile the history in code.** Cut the assistant message to the spoken prefix before the next LLM call. Do not ask the LLM to detect the cut.
6. **Mask tool latency.** Run a slow tool asynchronously, so that the agent can keep talking. Set the threshold from measurements of your tools. Keep a pre-synthesized hold message ready, so that it plays without TTS latency and stops when the tool returns. A remark while the user waits must not report a result, say that the work is done, or make a promise.
7. **Classify each tool.** A read-only lookup can be interrupted, and its result stays in the history. A write needs a cancellation check before its commit step, or it must be uninterruptible. Tell the caller when a step cannot be cancelled.
8. **Watch three metrics.** Count the cut-off user turns, the false interruptions, and the time from barge-in to silence.
9. **Compose with the neighbors.** [Agent Circuit Breaker](agent-circuit-breaker.md) stops repeated calls to a dead tool, which cause repeated dead air. [Spectrum of Control / Blended Initiative](spectrum-of-control-blended-initiative.md) applies to speech also: mark an utterance uninterruptible when it must play in full. For the reasoning that continues after a barge-in, see [Dual-Speed Realtime Architecture (Talker-Reasoner)](dual-speed-talker-reasoner-architecture.md).

## Trade-offs

**Pros:**

- Users can correct the agent in the middle of a sentence, not after the reply.
- The conversation history agrees with what the user heard, so later replies stay coherent.
- A slow tool no longer sounds like a dropped call.
- Each loop has its own metric, so a team can tune one loop without the others.

**Cons:**

- End-of-turn accuracy costs latency: a longer endpointing delay gives fewer cut-offs and slower replies.
- The pipeline runs more models (VAD, turn detector, interruption classifier), and some of them have separate licenses.
- The quality depends on the client. Echo cancellation runs in the client, and telephony has no browser to do it.
- Playout tracking, cancellation, and history truncation must hold in each frame processor, which makes the pipeline harder to change.

### Failure modes

- **The agent interrupts itself.** The agent stops speaking a moment after it starts, and nobody else is in the room. The cause is its own TTS output: the microphone picks up the speaker, and the echo reaches the VAD as user speech when the echo cancellation of the client fails or when a caller uses a speakerphone. Cancel the echo before the audio leaves the client, require transcribed words before an interruption counts, and resume the reply after a false interruption.
- **Phantom context.** The agent says "as I mentioned earlier" about words that it never spoke, or it never returns to the cut-off part of an answer. The cause is the complete reply in the conversation history while the user heard a prefix of it. Truncate the assistant message to the played prefix in code, at the moment of the interruption.
- **A backchannel stops the agent.** The user says "uh-huh" to show that they follow, and the agent stops. The cause is a VAD-only trigger that counts each speech as an interruption. Use adaptive interruption detection, set a minimum word count or speech duration, and resume after a false interruption.
- **An orphaned tool call.** The user says "actually, never mind, do not book it", and the booking completes. The cause is a tool that continues after the interruption, because an interruption of the agent does not cancel the work. Pass a cancellation signal into each tool, test it before the commit step, and make a write that cannot be rolled back uninterruptible.

## References

- [Pipecat](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat): open-source Python framework for real-time voice and multimodal agents, with interruption frames, VAD, and end-of-turn analyzers.
- [LiveKit Agents](https://github.com/livekit/agents): open-source framework for realtime voice AI agents, with semantic turn detection.
- [LiveKit Agents documentation](https://docs.livekit.io/agents/): turn detection, endpointing, interruptions, and tool-call handling.
- Related: [Chain-of-Thought Monitoring & Interruption](chain-of-thought-monitoring-interruption.md) (the stop signal on the text side), [Spectrum of Control / Blended Initiative](spectrum-of-control-blended-initiative.md) (selects what the user can interrupt), [Agent Circuit Breaker](agent-circuit-breaker.md) (stops repeated calls to a dead tool), [Dual-Speed Realtime Architecture (Talker-Reasoner)](dual-speed-talker-reasoner-architecture.md) (the background reasoning that a barge-in must cancel)

## Workflow Evals with Mocked Tools

**Status:** production
**Category:** Reliability & Eval
**Authors:** Nikola Balic (@nibzard)
**Source:** https://lethain.com/agents-evals/

## Problem

Unit tests, linters, and typecheckers validate individual components but do not test agent workflows end to end. It is easy to create prompts that do not work well although every underlying piece is correct. You need to validate that prompts and tools work together effectively as a system.

## Solution

Implement **workflow evals (simulations)** that test complete agent workflows with mocked tools. The approach is Sierra-inspired and has four components.

**1. Dual tool implementations.** Every tool has both a `true` and a `mock` version:

```python
# True implementation: calls the real API
def search_knowledge_base_true(query: str) -> str:
    return kb_api.search(query)

# Mock implementation: returns static test data
def search_knowledge_base_mock(query: str) -> str:
    return TEST_KB_RESULTS.get(query, DEFAULT_RESULT)
```

**2. Simulation configuration.** Each eval defines the initial prompt, metadata (situation context available to the harness), and evaluation criteria:

```yaml
evals:
  - name: slack_reaction_jira_workflow
    initial_prompt: "Add a smiley reaction to the JIRA ticket in this Slack message"
    metadata:
      situation: "slack_message_with_jira_link"
    evaluation_criteria:
      objective:
        - tools_called: ["slack_get_message", "jira_get_ticket", "slack_add_reaction"]
        - tools_not_called: ["slack_send_message"]
      subjective:
        - agent_judge: "Response was helpful and accurate"
```

**3. Dual evaluation criteria.** Objective criteria check which tools were called, which tools were not called, and which tags or states the conversation gained (if applicable). Subjective criteria use agent-as-judge assessments (for example, "Was the response friendly?") and LLM evaluations of qualitative outcomes.

**4. CI/CD integration.** A run loads the eval configuration, swaps in the mock implementations for all tools, runs the agent with the prompt and metadata, and tracks the tool calls. It then evaluates the objective criteria, runs the agent-as-judge for the subjective criteria, and reports pass or fail with details. CI triggers the run on every PR.

## Evidence

- **Evidence Grade:** `medium` - Independent practitioner report plus vendor-published evaluation frameworks (2026)
- **Key Findings:**
  - Strong production use case: unit tests and linters don't validate prompt-tool integration effectively
  - Dual evaluation (objective + subjective) is standard across implementations
  - Anthropic's "Demystifying evals for AI agents" (January 2026) codifies the grading side: code-based, model-based, and human graders applied to the trajectory or the final answer, which is the trajectory-level extension of this pattern
  - Non-determinism remains the primary challenge; best used for directional guidance
- **Unclear:** Optimal mock fidelity requirements for valid evaluation

## How to use it

**Best for:** agent workflows where tools have side effects (APIs, databases), CI/CD pipelines that need workflow validation, prompt engineering and optimization, and regression testing for agent behavior changes.

**1. Create a mock layer for tools:**

```python
class MockToolRegistry:
    def __init__(self, mode: str = "mock"):
        self.mode = mode
        self.mocks = {"slack_send_message": mock_slack_send_message, "jira_create_ticket": mock_jira_create_ticket}

    def get_tool(self, tool_name: str):
        return self.mocks[tool_name] if self.mode == "mock" else self.real_tools[tool_name]
```

**2. Define eval cases:**

```python
evals = [{
    "name": "login_support_flow",
    "prompt": "User can't log in, help them",
    "expected_tools": ["user_lookup", "password_reset"],
    "forbidden_tools": ["account_delete"],
    "subjective_criteria": "Response was empathetic and helpful",
}]
```

**3. Run and evaluate:**

```python
def run_eval(eval_config, mock_registry):
    result = agent.run(prompt=eval_config["prompt"], tools=mock_registry)
    tools_called = result.tools_used

    # Objective: tool usage
    passed = all(t in tools_called for t in eval_config["expected_tools"])
    passed &= all(t not in tools_called for t in eval_config["forbidden_tools"])

    # Subjective: agent-as-judge, only if the objective checks passed
    if passed:
        criteria = eval_config['subjective_criteria']
        passed = llm_evaluator(f"Evaluate this agent response: {result.response}\nCriteria: {criteria}\nPass/fail?") == "PASS"

    return {"passed": passed, "details": result}
```

**4. Integrate with CI/CD and post the results as a PR comment:**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/agent_evals.yml
name: Agent Evals
on: pull_request
jobs:
  evals:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: python scripts/run_evals.py --format github   # writes eval_results.json
      - uses: actions/github-script@v6                   # then posts it as a PR comment
```

**Handling non-determinism:**

The article notes that the evals work "not nearly as well as I hoped it would" because of non-determinism:

- **Strong signal**: all pass or all fail
- **Weak signal**: mixed results
- **Mitigation**: retry failed evals (for example, "at least once in three tries")

## Trade-offs

**Pros:**

- **End-to-end validation**: tests prompts and tools together as a system
- **Fast feedback**: catches regressions before they reach production
- **Safe testing**: mocked tools avoid side effects during testing
- **Clear criteria**: objective (tool calls) and subjective (quality) measures
- **CI/CD integration**: automated validation on every PR

**Cons:**

- **Non-deterministic**: LLM variability makes flaky tests common
- **Mock maintenance and tuning overhead**: mocks must stay in sync with real tool behavior, and prompts and mock responses need continuous adjustment
- **Limited signal**: mixed pass/fail results provide ambiguous guidance

**Operational challenges:**

> "Ok, this is working well, but not nearly as well as I hoped it would... there's very strong signal when they all fail, and strong signal when they all pass, but most runs are in between."

> "Our reliance on prompt-driven workflows rather than code-driven workflows introduces a lot of non-determinism, which I don't have a way to solve without... prompt and mock tuning."

**Failure modes / gotchas:**

- **Hard CI gate:** non-determinism makes evals flaky, so a strict gate blocks PRs at random. Use the results as directional context, and retry failures ("at least once in three tries").
- **Prompt-driven fragility:** prompt-driven workflows are more flaky than code-driven ones. Move complex workflows from prompts into code.
- **Mock drift:** a mock that no longer matches the real tool passes evals that fail in production. Tune mocks to be realistic and keep them synced.
- **Judge noise:** a vague subjective criterion adds more variance. Tune eval prompts to be precise and deterministic.

## References

* [Building an internal agent: Evals to validate workflows](https://lethain.com/agents-evals/) - Will Larson (December 2025)
* [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) - Anthropic Engineering (January 2026); code-based, model-based, and human graders over trajectories or final answers
* Sierra platform: Simulations approach for agent testing
* [LangSmith Evaluation Platform](https://smith.langchain.com/) - Tool tracking and custom evaluators
* [Promptfoo](https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo) - Mock API responses and assertion-based testing
* Related: [Stop Hook Auto-Continue Pattern](stop-hook-auto-continue-pattern.md) - Post-execution testing
* Related: [Agent Reinforcement Fine-Tuning](agent-reinforcement-fine-tuning.md) - Training on agent workflows

## Working Memory via Task Tracking

**Status:** emerging
**Category:** Context & Memory
**Authors:** Nikola Balic (@nibzard)
**Source:** https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

## Problem

During complex multi-step tasks, AI agents lose track of:
- What tasks are pending, in progress, or completed
- Which tasks are blocked by dependencies
- Verification steps that need to run
- Next actions after context switches

This leads to redundant work, forgotten tasks, and confused users.

## Solution

Use session task-tracking tools (in Claude Code: `TaskCreate`, `TaskGet`, `TaskUpdate`, and `TaskList`; earlier versions exposed a single `TodoWrite` tool) to maintain explicit working memory throughout the session. This serves as both agent and user visibility into session state.

**Theoretical foundation:** Externalizes working memory per Baddeley's episodic buffer model and Miller's 7±2 capacity limit—humans and LLMs both struggle to track more than a handful of items internally.

**What to track:**

1. **Task status**: pending, in_progress, completed
2. **Blocking relationships**: What blocks what
3. **Verification steps**: Tests or checks needed
4. **Next actions**: What to do next

**Usage patterns from the author's session analysis** (self-reported; the repository that hosted the analysis is no longer online, so treat the table as anecdotal):

| Project | Task-list uses | Session quality |
|---------|---------------|-----------------|
| nibzard-web | 52 | High (8 positive, 2 corrections) |
| awesome-agentic-patterns | 60 | Medium (1 positive, 5 corrections) |
| marginshot | 36 | No feedback captured |
| 2025-intro-swe | 0 | Simple work, no need |

**Key insights:**

- In that (unverifiable) analysis, task-list use accompanied smoother sessions; this is an observation, not a controlled result
- It serves as working memory for both agent and user
- Essential for complex multi-step tasks
- Less critical for simple, straightforward work

**Current tooling note:** since Claude Code v2.1.268 (Agent SDK v0.3.268), newer models track multi-step work without a written todo list, so todo tools are opt-in (`CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`), mainly to render progress for the user; the legacy `TodoWrite` tool remains only as a fallback (`CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TASKS=0`). The underlying practice — externalizing task state for long-horizon work — is still recommended in Anthropic's context engineering guidance.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending: Task identified
    Pending --> InProgress: Started
    InProgress --> Completed: Finished
    InProgress --> Blocked: Dependency wait
    Blocked --> InProgress: Dependency resolved
    Completed --> [*]

    note right of Pending
        Create via task tool
        with clear subject
    end note

    note right of InProgress
        Update status to
        track progress
    end note

    note right of Blocked
        Document blocking
        relationships
    end note
```

## How to use it

**When to use:**

- Working on complex multi-step tasks
- Need to track blocked tasks and dependencies
- Want to maintain session state across operations
- Multiple parallel work streams

**Implementation approach:**

1. **Create tasks proactively**: When you identify work, create a task entry
2. **Update status as you go**: Mark tasks in_progress when starting
3. **Maintain single active task**: Exactly ONE task should be in_progress at a time
4. **Document dependencies**: Use `blocks`/`blockedBy` relationships
5. **Mark complete when done**: Only mark tasks completed when truly finished
6. **Keep descriptions clear**: Include enough context for future reference

**Example workflow:**

```
1. User: "Add OAuth login and fix the search bug"
2. Agent creates 2 tasks with the task-tracking tool
3. Agent marks OAuth task in_progress, starts work
4. Agent realizes OAuth needs database schema change
5. Agent blocks OAuth task, creates schema task
6. Agent completes schema, unblocks OAuth
7. Agent completes OAuth, moves to search bug
8. Agent completes search, marks all done
```

**Anti-pattern prevention:**

- Prevents context loss across context window switches
- Prevents redundant work (doing same task twice)
- Prevents forgotten tasks (user asks "what about X?")
- Prevents unclear session state

## Trade-offs

**Pros:**

- Explicit session state for agent and user
- Dependency tracking prevents blocked work
- Progress visibility builds confidence
- Survives context window switches
- Reduces "what about X?" questions from users

**Cons:**

- Overhead for simple tasks
- Requires discipline to maintain
- Can become cluttered if overused
- May feel bureaucratic for quick one-offs

**When NOT to use:**

- Simple, single-step tasks
- Tasks that complete in seconds
- When user just wants quick answers

## References

* [Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents) (Anthropic) — recommends agentic memory such as notes and todo lists for long-horizon tasks, including Claude Code's to-do list
* [Todo tracking (Claude Agent SDK docs)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/todo-tracking) — current behavior: task-tracking tools by model, opt-in flags, and the `TodoWrite` legacy fallback (replaces the dead `docs.anthropic.com` task-lists page)
* Original evidence base: the author's 88-session Claude analysis (`github.com/nibzard/SKILLS-AGENTIC-LESSONS`) is no longer available (HTTP 404), so the usage table above cannot be independently verified
* Related patterns: [Proactive Agent State Externalization](proactive-agent-state-externalization.md), [Filesystem-Based Agent State](filesystem-based-agent-state.md)
* Baddeley, A. (2000). "The Episodic Buffer: A New Component of Working Memory?" *Trends in Cognitive Sciences*, 4(11), 417-423.
* Miller, G. A. (1956). "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two." *Psychological Review*, 63(2), 81-97.

## Workspace-Native Multi-Agent Orchestration

**Status:** proposed
**Category:** Orchestration & Control
**Authors:** John Xie (@johnxie)
**Source:** https://doi.org/10.1609/aimag.v7i2.537

## Problem

Many teams struggle to run agentic workflows because their agent tooling is separate from their day-to-day collaboration environment. The result is fragmented context, brittle integrations, and high setup overhead.

Common pain points include:

- Agents are difficult to create and version for non-engineering users.
- Context, memory, and knowledge sources are spread across ad hoc systems.
- Multi-agent workflows require custom glue for routing, event triggers, and state transfer.
- Integrating agents with operational tools (issue trackers, docs, chat, CRM) is expensive.

## Solution

The pattern is to make agents native participants in the workspace platform itself, so they share the same context, memory, and lifecycle as human collaborators. This approach builds on established patterns like blackboard architecture (shared memory for coordination) and tuple spaces (associative addressing for decoupled communication).

**Core components:**

1. **Agent definitions are shared, versioned artifacts**: each agent has role/constraints/tool access defined in one place.
2. **Shared workspace memory**: persistent, team-curated sources (documents, URLs, files) feed agent context. Memory types include episodic (past executions), semantic (knowledge base), and procedural (capabilities and tools).
3. **Workflow orchestration inside the workspace**: outputs from one agent can trigger downstream agents via event-driven workflows. Trigger patterns include direct (event → action), conditional (event + condition → action), composite (multiple events → action), and temporal (event + delay → action).
4. **Standardized integration surface**: expose tools/actions through a consistent protocol layer (for example MCP-compatible tool interfaces).
5. **Cross-platform accessibility**: keep behavior consistent across web, desktop, mobile, and browser contexts.

```mermaid
graph TD
  A[User task/trigger] --> B[Workspace state + memory]
  B --> C[Agent workflow coordinator]
  C --> D1[Agent A: Research]
  C --> D2[Agent B: Synthesis]
  C --> D3[Agent C: Delivery]
  D1 --> B
  D2 --> B
  D3 --> E[Tool integrations / external actions]
```

## How to use it

- Start with one use-case, then scale to more complex agent handoffs.
- Define a clear contract per agent (scope, outputs, allowed tools).
- Use shared memory sources and update them programmatically when workflows complete.
- Keep trigger graph small at first; expand to chained agents only where dependencies are clear.
- Prefer protocol-based integrations so alternate agent runtimes can consume the same workspace actions.

## Trade-offs

- **Pros:**
  - Lowers onboarding friction for teams without heavy automation infrastructure.
  - Preserves context across sessions via shared, persistent workspace memory.
  - Improves handoff quality between agents and humans.
  - Reduces integration effort through standardized action surfaces.

- **Cons/considerations:**
  - Strong coupling to the chosen workspace platform.
  - Some advanced behaviors may still require custom agent code.
  - Workflow chains can become difficult to debug as they grow.
  - Operational dependency and governance requirements sit in platform settings.

## References

- Example implementation (vendor pages): [Taskade AI Agents](https://taskade.com/agents), [Taskade MCP Server](https://github.com/taskade/mcp)
- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) — open standard for the standardized integration surface above
- [Anthropic: Introducing the Model Context Protocol](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol)
- Nii, H. P. (1986). [Blackboard Systems: The Blackboard Model of Problem Solving and the Evolution of Blackboard Architectures](https://doi.org/10.1609/aimag.v7i2.537). AI Magazine.
- Gelernter, D. (1985). [Generative Communication in Linda](https://doi.org/10.1145/2363.2433). ACM TOPLAS.
- Related patterns: [Board-Mediated Async Inter-Agent Coordination](board-mediated-inter-agent-coordination.md) coordinates agents with each other through a shared board, while this pattern embeds agents in the human team workspace so people and agents share the same memory, triggers, and integrations.

## Zero-Knowledge Verified Agent Egress

**Status:** proposed
**Category:** Security & Safety
**Authors:** Provably (@aural-psynapse)
**Source:** https://github.com/ProvablyAI/sourcerykit

## Problem

An agent can be tricked into making an outbound request that looks fine at the network layer but carries a false claim: a payment to the wrong recipient, an API call with tampered parameters, a tool call whose arguments do not match what the user approved. A domain allow-list or egress firewall lets the call through because the destination is allowed; it never checks whether the *content* of the request is truthful. In regulated or high-value flows, teams need each outbound call to prove it matches a trusted source of truth before it leaves, without exposing that source of truth to the agent or the destination.

## Solution

Put a verification layer in front of every outbound request. Before the call leaves, the agent's claims about it get checked against a source of truth, and a zero-knowledge proof confirms the claims hold without revealing the underlying data. The call only goes out if the proof verifies.

The layer wraps the agent's HTTP path and MCP handoffs:

1. **Intercept**: hook the HTTP libraries the agent already uses, plus MCP tool calls, so every outbound request passes through.
2. **Verify**: check the request's claims against the source of truth and produce a zero-knowledge proof that they match. The proof runs against a backend that holds the source of truth, so neither the agent nor the destination sees it.
3. **Enforce**: block anything whose proof does not verify, and block any endpoint not on the trusted allow-list. Log every outbound call for audit.

```pseudo
on_outbound_request(req):
    proof = prove_against_source_of_truth(req.claims)   # zero-knowledge
    if not verify(proof):        return BLOCK
    if req.endpoint not in allow_list:  return BLOCK
    log(req, proof)
    return ALLOW
```

This is complementary to [Egress Lockdown (No-Exfiltration Channel)](egress-lockdown-no-exfiltration-channel.md): that pattern controls *where* an agent may send data at the network layer, while this one verifies that *what* the agent is sending is true before it goes. It also differs from [Policy-Gated Tool Proxy](policy-gated-tool-proxy.md): the proxy decides whether a call is *allowed* against static policy rules, while this pattern proves the call's *content* matches a private source of truth at egress time.

## Evidence

- **Evidence Grade:** medium
- **Most Valuable Findings:**
  - NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture) establishes per-request verification before granting access as a core tenet; this pattern applies the same tenet to an agent's outbound calls. NIST SP 800-207 does not mention agents or egress content verification, so it serves as a conceptual basis, not a description of this pattern.
  - Zero-knowledge proofs let a verifier confirm a claim without seeing the secret behind it (Goldwasser, Micali & Rackoff, 1989), so the source of truth stays private from both the agent and the destination.
  - Agent-security literature treats untrusted tool calls and prompt-injection-driven misuse as a first-class problem (see "A Survey on Agentic Security", arXiv:2510.06445; OWASP's Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations guide; and CaMeL, "Defeating Prompt Injections by Design", arXiv:2503.18813, which enforces security policies when tools are invoked through a capability mechanism). None of these describes content verification via zero-knowledge proofs at egress.
  - Hooking at the HTTP and MCP layer catches outbound calls regardless of which framework produced them.
- **Unverified / Unclear:** Proof-generation latency and the operational cost of running the verification backend at high call volumes need more production data.
- **Adoption caveat:** the only known implementation is from the pattern author's own company; no third-party deployment, adoption, or independent writeup exists yet.

## How to use it

- Wrap any agent framework that makes outbound HTTP or MCP tool calls (LangChain, CrewAI, MCP servers, custom SDKs) so every outbound request passes through the verification layer.
- Define the source of truth for the flows that matter (approved recipients, order details, policy limits) and a trusted-endpoint allow-list.
- Pick a proof mechanism: a zero-knowledge proof keeps the source of truth private from both the agent and the destination; where privacy is not a constraint, a signed attestation from the verifier achieves the same gating.
- Route outbound calls through the layer; treat a failed proof or a non-allowlisted endpoint as a hard block.
- Keep the signed logs for audit and incident review.

An existing implementation of this pattern is [SourceryKit](https://github.com/ProvablyAI/sourcerykit) (Python SDK, source-available under Business Source License 1.1, converting to GPL-3.0-or-later in 2029). Disclosure: it is the pattern author's own product — the Python SDK for Provably — and it depends on Provably's hosted backend, which holds the source of truth and produces the anchored verification proofs; interception happens locally, but verification is not fully offline.

## Trade-offs

- **Pros:** Catches truthful-looking but false requests that a network allow-list misses; the source of truth stays private via the zero-knowledge proof; framework-agnostic through HTTP and MCP hooks; every call is logged.
- **Cons:** Proof generation adds latency per call; verification runs against a backend rather than fully offline; someone has to define and maintain the source of truth for each flow.

## References

- [SourceryKit](https://github.com/ProvablyAI/sourcerykit) (implementation; pattern origin)
- [NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final) (conceptual basis)
- [Goldwasser, Micali & Rackoff: The Knowledge Complexity of Interactive Proof Systems (SIAM J. Comput., 1989)](https://doi.org/10.1137/0218012)
- [A Survey on Agentic Security (arXiv:2510.06445)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06445)
- [Debenedetti et al., "Defeating Prompt Injections by Design" (CaMeL, arXiv:2503.18813)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.18813)
- [OWASP GenAI Security Project: Agentic AI - Threats and Mitigations](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/agentic-ai-threats-and-mitigations/)
- [Egress Lockdown (No-Exfiltration Channel)](egress-lockdown-no-exfiltration-channel.md)
- [Policy-Gated Tool Proxy](policy-gated-tool-proxy.md)

## Zero-Trust Agent Mesh

**Status:** emerging
**Category:** Security & Safety
**Authors:** Imran Siddique (@imran-siddique)
**Source:** https://www.nist.gov/publications/zero-trust-architecture

## Problem

In multi-agent systems, trust boundaries are often implicit: agents communicate by convention without verifiable identity, and delegation chains are hard to audit. This enables impersonation, privilege confusion, and unverifiable task delegation.

## Solution

Apply zero-trust principles to inter-agent communication:

- **Agent identities are cryptographically asserted** (Ed25519 key pairs per agent for fast signatures with 64-byte size).
- **Mutual trust handshakes** confirm identity before requests are accepted.
- **Delegation tokens** carry signed scope, TTL, and parent authority.
- **Bounded delegation** limits chain depth and blast radius.

Every request is evaluated as an untrusted call until identity, authorization, and delegation lineage are verified. Policies are enforced per hop, not just at the edge, and verification results are logged as first-class audit events. This turns "agent collaboration" into a traceable authorization graph rather than a trust-by-convention channel.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Agent A
    participant M as Trust Verifier
    participant B as Agent B
    A->>M: Register key / identity
    B->>M: Register key / identity
    A->>B: Challenge nonce
    B->>A: Signed challenge response
    A->>A: Verify response
    A->>B: Delegation token (scoped + TTL)
    B->>M: Present chain for approval
    M->>M: Verify signature + chain depth
```

## Evidence

- **Evidence Grade:** `medium`
- **Most Valuable Findings:**
  - Workload identity at scale is proven infrastructure: SPIFFE/SPIRE joined CNCF in 2018, moved to incubating on 2020-06-22, and graduated on 2022-08-23 — but for service meshes and general workloads, not yet for production agent meshes
  - The underlying primitives are standardized: NIST SP 800-207 defines per-request verification, and Ed25519 signatures are cheap enough for per-hop verification
  - Inter-agent protocol support is arriving but incomplete: A2A (26k+ stars) still lists authorization schemes as future work
- **Unverified / Unclear:** Native zero-trust support in major agent frameworks remains adapter-based, not first-class; no published benchmark measures the verification overhead of full identity-plus-delegation checks per inter-agent hop



## How to use it

- Enable trust checks for every inter-agent request, not just sensitive ones.
- Keep delegation scopes narrowly scoped and short-lived.
- Require explicit expiry and refresh for long-running tasks.
- Centralize verifier policy (TTL defaults, trust score decay, blocklist/allowlist).

## Trade-offs

- Adds latency and additional components for key management and verification.
- Requires security operations discipline around key rotation and revocation.
- Trust scoring and policy tuning adds governance overhead.
- Existing agent frameworks need adapter glue.

## References

- [NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-207/final)
- Beurer-Kellner et al. (2025). "Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections" [arXiv:2506.08837](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2506.08837)
- Greshake et al. (2023). "Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications" [arXiv:2302.12173](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2302.12173)
- [SPIFFE/SPIRE](https://spiffe.io/) and the [CNCF project page](https://www.cncf.io/projects/spiffe/) — graduated 2022-08-23
- [Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-governance-toolkit) — includes the AgentMesh component as one part of a broader governance toolkit (Public Preview)
- [A2A Protocol](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A) — inter-agent protocol; formalizing authorization schemes in the AgentCard is on its roadmap, not shipped
- Adjacent pattern: [Transitive Vouch-Chain Trust](transitive-vouch-chain-trust.md) — derives trust from signed vouches between peers rather than verifying a cryptographic identity on every request
- Adjacent pattern: [Soulbound Identity Verification](soulbound-identity-verification.md) — binds identity to a non-transferable credential for continuity, complementing per-request verification here
